Jerusalem, a few days before Passover, the great spring festival of the Jewish people.
The courtyards of the temple, the centre of Jewish worship, are crowded with pilgrims.
A teacher from Galilee named Jesus is sitting among them, and people have gathered to listen.
A group of men make their way to the front.
They call Him Teacher, and they tell Him they know He is an honest man who teaches the way of God truthfully.
Then they ask their question.
Is it right to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?
Caesar was the Roman emperor.
Rome had conquered the Jewish homeland, its soldiers kept order in Jerusalem, and the people groaned under the occupation.
Every tax they paid reminded them who ruled them.
So everyone listening could see the trap.
If Jesus said yes, He would lose the crowd.
If He said no, He was calling for a tax revolt, and the Roman soldiers were a short walk away.
Jesus asked to see the coin used for the tax.
Someone handed Him a denarius, a small Roman silver coin, worn smooth by many hands.
He held it up.
On one side was the head of the emperor of the day, Tiberius.
The words around it called him son of the divine Augustus, the emperor before him, whom Rome honoured as a god.
The other side called Tiberius highest priest.
In one small piece of metal, a man claimed to rule the world and to stand between people and heaven.
"Whose image is this?"
Jesus asked.
"And whose inscription?"
"Caesar's," they said.
"Then give back to Caesar what is Caesar's," He said, "and to God what is God's."
The men who had come to trap Him were amazed.
They left Him and went away.
The coin carried Caesar's face, so it belonged to Caesar, and he could have it back.
That leads to a second question.
Whose face do you carry?
Every man in that courtyard had learned the first page of the Scriptures as a boy.
"So God created mankind in His own image; in the image of God He created them."
Christians since the earliest days of the church have heard that verse behind Jesus' words.
If the coin with Caesar's image belongs to Caesar, then the person with God's image belongs to God.
That means you, every part of you, on every day of the week.
